title: Atoms, isotopes and ions: count particles before naming the species
author: Assistant

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism

objectives: Identify the particles that determine element, isotope and ionic charge.
Calculate neutrons and electrons from a nuclide symbol.
Distinguish a model of an atom from a scaled picture.
prerequisites: An electric charge may be positive, negative or zero; opposite charges attract.
An element is a substance identified by a particular number of protons.

terms.nucleus: The small central region containing protons and, in most atoms, neutrons.
terms.nucleon: A proton or neutron in the nucleus.
terms.ion: An atom or group of atoms with a net charge.

conceptualTeaching.explanation: An atom contains a small nucleus and electrons occupying the surrounding region. A proton has positive charge, a neutron is uncharged and an electron has an equal-magnitude negative charge. Nearly all atomic mass is associated with the nucleus. A diagram that shows separate dots is a counting model; it does not show real particle sizes or the quantum distribution of electrons.

Atomic number Z equals the number of protons and fixes the element. Mass number A counts protons plus neutrons, so N=A−Z. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have Z=6. Their neutron counts are 12−6=6 and 14−6=8. They are isotopes, not separate elements. Mass number is an integer count for a nuclide; it is not the periodic table’s abundance-weighted average atomic mass.

In a neutral atom the positive and negative charges balance, so electrons equal protons. Losing an electron creates a positive ion; gaining one creates a negative ion. If q is the signed charge in elementary-charge units, electron count is Z−q. Thus a species with Z=11 and q=+1 has 10 electrons. Changing electron count does not change Z or A. By contrast, changing neutron number changes the isotope.

visualUnderstanding.description: Show separate labelled counts for protons, neutrons and electrons. Toggle carbon-12/carbon-14 while holding Z=6, then toggle charge while holding nucleons fixed.
visualUnderstanding.limitations: Not to scale; no fixed planetary electron paths or prediction of isotope stability.

realWorldApplication.example: For a species with A=23, Z=11 and charge +1: protons=11, neutrons=12 and electrons=10. Check the charge independently: 11−10=+1.

examinationApplication.prompt: Using carbon-12 and carbon-14, distinguish an isotope from an ion. Show how proton, neutron and electron counts determine the difference.

questions.prompt: Two neutral atoms each have six protons. One has six neutrons and the other eight. Which statement is correct?

options.C: They have different numbers of electrons.
options.D: The heavier atom must have a positive charge.

optionExplanations.A: The element is fixed by proton number; both have six.
optionExplanations.B: Equal proton numbers and different neutron numbers define isotopes of the same element.
optionExplanations.C: Both are neutral, so each has six electrons.
optionExplanations.D: Neutrons add no charge, so the additional neutrons do not make a positive ion.

questions.prompt: A sodium species has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons. What are its mass number and charge?

optionExplanations.A: Mass number is 11+12=23; charge is 11−10=+1 in elementary-charge units.
optionExplanations.B: Subtracting an electron does not change mass number, which counts nucleons only.
optionExplanations.C: There are more protons than electrons, so the net charge is positive.
optionExplanations.D: 11 is the atomic number, and the unequal proton/electron counts mean the species is not neutral.

questions.prompt: An atom loses one electron. Which quantity necessarily changes?

optionExplanations.A: Atomic number is proton number and remains unchanged.
optionExplanations.B: An electronic change does not remove or add a neutron.
optionExplanations.C: Mass number counts protons and neutrons, neither of which changes.
optionExplanations.D: Removing negative charge makes the net charge one elementary charge more positive.

answerWriting.modelResponse: Atomic number Z is the number of protons and identifies an element. Mass number A is the number of protons plus neutrons, so N=A−Z. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons but have six and eight neutrons respectively; they are isotopes of carbon. A neutral atom has equal proton and electron counts. An ion forms when this charge balance changes through electron loss or gain: a carbon species with six protons and five electrons has charge +1, while its isotope identity is still determined by its neutron count. Therefore isotope differences concern neutrons; ionic charge concerns the balance of protons and electrons.

rubric.criterion: Define atomic number and mass number correctly.
Calculate six versus eight neutrons for the two carbon isotopes.
Explain why both remain the same element.
Explain electron loss/gain and the sign of ionic charge.
Make a direct isotope-versus-ion distinction using a correct example.

commonMistakes: Adding electron mass to the integer mass number.
